summary: Describes mistakes often found in DNS data files, explaining what system administrators commonly get wrong and why such errors can go unnoticed for a long time. It was replaced by RFC 1912.

eli5.summary: Little typos in the Internet's phone book can hide for ages. This memo lists the usual typos and why nobody sees them.

questions: what are common dns configuration mistakes
how should dns timers be set
why does dns sometimes break silently
subtitle: Common mistakes system administrators make when writing DNS zone files.

tldr.problem: System administrators configure DNS zone files by hand, and subtle rules lead to common mistakes that often go unnoticed for long periods.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1537 describes the mistakes most often seen: improper timers in SOA records, unnecessary or wrong glue records, misconfigured secondary servers, MX record problems, unintended name extensions, wildcard MX pitfalls, hostname format errors, and incomplete HINFO records.
tldr.outcome: By learning these mistakes, administrators can avoid silent DNS failures and unnecessary traffic. The RFC was later replaced by RFC 1912 which updates and expands the guidance.

today: RFC 1537 is an Informational document published in October 1993 and was obsoleted by RFC 1912 in February 1995, which expands and updates the guidance on DNS configuration mistakes.

sections.title: Why DNS Mistakes Hide
sections.content:
DNS zone files are written by system administrators by hand, guided by subtle rules in RFCs and manuals. A few common mistakes appear worldwide and go undetected for long periods because the DNS system does not always fail loudly when something is wrong.

This RFC catalogs the "surprises" administrators often discover hidden in their zone files, describing the symptoms and remedies for each type of error.
sections.eli5: DNS zone files have tricky rules that are easy to mess up, and when you do mess up, nobody notices right away.

sections.title: SOA Records and Timing Mistakes
sections.content:
The Start of Authority (SOA) record contains four timers that control how secondary nameservers refresh zone data, retry failed transfers, and expire information when the primary is unreachable. The problem is that common examples (in RFCs, manuals, and BIND documentation) recommend values that are far too low.

For top-level domain servers, recommended Refresh is 86400 seconds (24 hours), Retry is 7200 seconds (2 hours), Expire is 2592000 seconds (30 days), and Minimum TTL is 345600 seconds (4 days). For other servers, Refresh should be 28800 seconds (8 hours), Retry 7200, Expire 604800 (7 days), and Minimum TTL 86400 (1 day). Setting these too low causes unnecessary international traffic as secondaries constantly check for updates.
sections.eli5: The SOA record tells secondary servers how often to check for updates. If you set the numbers too low, your DNS servers will be constantly chatting with each other, which is wasteful.

sections.title: Names, Glue, and Wildcards
sections.content:
Administrators often include unnecessary glue records (A records for nameservers within their zone) or even wrong glue records for external hosts. Glue records are only needed when the nameserver itself lives within the zone. Worse, old BIND versions could transfer wrong glue records to secondary servers.

Another common mistake is forgetting to terminate domain names with a dot, which causes names to be automatically expanded with the current zone name. For example, in zone foo.xx, an MX record for relay.yy becomes relay.yy.foo.xx instead of relay.yy.

Wildcard MX records cause confusion because a host with any explicit record type is NOT covered by the wildcard, not even if the explicit record is only for another record type. Many administrators expect wildcards to apply to all record types, leading to mail routing errors.
sections.eli5: Small typos in domain names cause big problems. A missing dot or too many extra records can send mail to the wrong place.

sections.title: Secondary Servers and Configuration Surprises
sections.content:
Sometimes hosts get bombarded by nameserver queries without their administrators knowing why—it turns out registrars had registered them as secondary servers without asking permission or informing anyone. Newer BIND versions solved this problem, but it became harder to spot because servers silently rejected the registration.

Secondary servers should have at least 2 per domain, with more for top-level domains at strategic global locations. A recommended maximum is 7 nameservers for any domain. Additionally, secondary nameservers should always transfer zones directly from the official primary server, not from another secondary, to avoid cascading TTL errors.

When registering subdomains, top-level domain managers should sanity-check the new nameserver before adding NS records, verifying that SOA timers are reasonable, required MX records exist, and secondary servers are actually operational.
sections.eli5: You need at least two nameservers for each domain, and they need to be in different places so the Internet can find them. Getting this wrong means the whole domain becomes unreachable.

sections.title: Record Format and Safety Measures
sections.content:
Hostnames must conform to the DNS syntax in RFC 1034, not just RFC 822 rules for email addresses. Characters like ampersand and hyphen may be legal in email addresses but cause serious problems in hostnames on Unix systems (for example, telnet c&w.blues has unexpected shell interpretation).

HINFO records have two mandatory fields (hardware type and software type); incomplete HINFO records with only one field are invalid, though HINFO records themselves are optional.

All nameservers should run primary for the 0.in-addr.arpa, 255.in-addr.arpa, and 127.0.0.1 reverse zones to catch bogus queries locally and avoid unnecessary traffic to the root servers. A PTR record for 127.0.0.1 should point to localhost. (with the trailing dot).

Serial numbers should use date notation (yyyymmdd or yyyymmddn) rather than Release.Version notation, because of a bug in all BIND versions: dotted decimal serial numbers are calculated wrong, making it virtually impossible to increment the release number.
sections.eli5: DNS records have strict rules about what characters are allowed and what fields are required. Sloppy data in DNS can break the whole Internet's navigation system.

sections.title: Naming Authority Responsibilities
sections.content:
DNS naming authorities act as clearing houses: anyone registering a subdomain becomes the naming authority for that subdomain and is solely responsible for it. Therefore, registrars MUST honor all requests for MX or NS records for a subdomain, regardless of what was previously there.

Forbidden practices include imposing specific mail routing when registering a subdomain, making registration dependent on use of certain networks or services, and using TXT records for commercial advertising. A network operator can cut off a domain until such records are removed.

Naming authorities may refuse a subdomain registration only on exceptional grounds (like DEC trying to register domain IBM), and must verify that the applicant has authority to register (not every department head should register a whole university domain).
sections.eli5: When you register a domain name, you are responsible for managing it correctly. Nobody else can force you to route mail a certain way or use their services.
